newsitem.title: TURKEY: Secularist generals attack Islamist Turkish PM.
newsitem.headline: Secularist generals attack Islamist Turkish PM.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan is coming under increasing pressure from the secularist army, as generals intensify a verbal barrage against his government over the role of religion in public life.

A top general capped a series of attacks on the prime minister on Tuesday by warning that the military's struggle against Islamist activism was a "life and death" matter for officially secular Turkey.
The military's attitude has long been supported by media owners and is increasingly backed by law and order authorities.

Police in Ankara have arrested 21 people in a week for putting on an Islamist play deemed to have insulted the security forces. On Monday security forces said they had closed more than 20 buildings where Islamists were holding illegal Koranic lessons.
A preacher close to Erbakan's Welfare Party went on trial on Monday, charged with fostering religious separatism and hatred.
The legal assault on the Islamists is likely to continue on Wednesday, as members of an Islamic sect appear in court for a further hearing on charges of challenging secularism.
The Aczmendi sect have been criticised for wearing long Islamic robes -- outlawed under Turkey's secularist dress code -- and holding frenzied prayer meetings.
Under increasing pressure from the army and secularists, including the opposition, Erbakan on Tuesday threw down the gauntlet by threatening to hold early general elections.
"Today at any moment, whoever wants it, we are ready for elections," Erbakan told a meeting of his Welfare Party MPs.
Analysts say deputies from all parties are unwilling to risk their seats, and parliamentary privileges, at snap polls.
Erbakan, secularist Turkey's first Islamist leader, came to power in June at the head of a coalition with the conservatives of former premier Tansu Ciller, after elections in December 1995.
Ciller's side of the coalition -- on good terms with the army when she was prime minister -- has come under pressure to split with Welfare.
Two pro-Western ministers quit at the weekend in sympathy with army frustration over Erbakan's reluctance to carry out an army-inspired crackdown on Islamists.
At least one of the pair said he would rally colleagues uneasy with Welfare's behaviour in a bid to challenge Ciller.
Opposition leaders, too, held talks on Tuesday on ways to topple the government, but attempts at such alliances have often failed in the past due to personal rivalries.
Erbakan played down the conflict with the army after an impromptu meeting with armed forces chief Ismail Hakki Karadayi.
"As will be seen, the top ranks of the state are one, they are together. Our president, our government and our army are one body," he told reporters after the talks.
The generals, who have staged three coups since 1960, have led a chorus of secularist uproar against attempts by Erbakan to relax strict restrictions on the role of Islam.

They fear Welfare is planning to turn NATO member Turkey into an Islamic state like neighbouring Iran, but are unwilling to use force against the government for fear of jeopardising Turkey's prized ties to the West.
